items.summary: Anthropic's record-breaking IPO did not stop a broad decline in AI-linked stocks, as global equity markets fell sharply. Asian markets were on track for their worst week since 2020: Taiwan's index dropped 6.7% with TSMC down about 6%, Japan's Nikkei fell 5%, and South Korea's Kospi lost 5.5%. SoftBank shares fell 14.5% in Tokyo amid concerns over its AI bets, marking its worst day in more than two years. Europe was heading for its worst week since March, with the Stoxx 600 down 1.3% early Friday, and Britain's FTSE 100 hit a five-month low after dropping 4.8% on the week. The sell-off followed Wall Street losses Thursday when all main indices fell over 2%. Anthropic shares rose 17% at launch after briefly surging nearly 40%, but were heading for Friday losses, down 6% to $91.30 near the IPO price of $83. Daniela Hathorn of Capital.com said demand for AI exposure remained strong but was insufficient to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability, and sustainable investment spending; she noted that selling pressure had spread beyond a few technology giants and Europe's recent outperformance had faded.
items.title: Global stock markets slumped after Anthropic's IPO failed to halt an AI sell-off

items.summary: Deutsche Lufthansa plans to eliminate 1,000 full-time positions at Munich and Frankfurt hubs as part of an effort to reverse losses in the unprofitable Lufthansa Airlines mainline unit. The cuts are set out in a management letter seen by Bloomberg and accompany planned capacity reductions on short- and medium-haul routes plus a fleet shift from Airbus A320 aircraft to smaller A220s. These measures mark the second round of job cuts in slightly more than a year, following an announcement in September 2025 that the group would cut 4,000 administrative jobs by 2030. Lufthansa Airlines reported an operating loss of €180 million (S$254.8 million) over the first nine months, and management attributed worsening conditions to high jet-fuel prices, Middle East conflict, a nine-day strike period, and elevated costs. The measures were revealed on Nov 20 amid ongoing negotiations with labour unions, though no agreement has been reached.
items.title: Lufthansa to cut 1,000 jobs at its mainline airline unit

items.summary: US semiconductor equipment maker KLA opened Building 22B in Ang Mo Kio, giving it roughly 210,000 sq ft of new operational space; the site was announced in October 2024 and is now fully operational. The company has outlined plans for a further expansion phase that would be larger than this one, but those details are still being defined pending finalised land arrangements and approvals, so no third-phase commitment or timeline is established. Kneepkens said the next phase “will be bigger than the current expanded site.” Long-term, Building 22B and the planned phase could support about 1,000 new jobs across R&D, supply chain and manufacturing engineering; KLA Singapore currently employs over 2,200 people on multiple shifts. Higgins attributed growth to local talent, collaborative partners and supplier/customer access, and said demand is “only accelerating.” The expansion follows investment commitments from other semiconductor value-chain firms including GlobalFoundries, Micron, Siltronic, Soitec, UMC, Vanguard International Semiconductor and NXP Semiconductors. Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong noted Singapore accounts for around one-fifth of global production and has committed $800 million under the Research, Innovation and Enterprise 2030 plan to RIE Flagship in Semiconductors; he also cited a three-year KLA–A*STAR collaboration and local supplier Sys-Mac Automation Engineering. The opening was attended by Singapore Economic Development Board executive vice-president Cindy Koh.
items.title: KLA opens expanded Singapore plant with plans for a third expansion phase

items.summary: Freelance journalist Garrison Lovely, author of Obsolete: The AI Industry's Trillion-Dollar Race to Replace Us - And How to Stop It, contends that recent outages at Microsoft, United Airlines, JPMorgan Chase, the NSA network, European freezer hacks, and malware reaching 178 organizations including BBC, CNN, Zoom and HSBC show a porous digital-physical border with AI blamed for accelerating both cybercrime and software vulnerabilities. He attributes much of the surge to open-weight models from Chinese developers piggybacking on superhuman hacker AIs first built by Anthropic and OpenAI, which he says released guardrail-free versions knowing China would follow; these claims are presented as his argument rather than established fact. Citing a third-party evaluator's estimate that parts of Anthropic's development were already moving roughly twice as fast due to AI doing an increasing share of the work, Lovely calls for freezing frontier-AI and recursive self-improvement efforts aimed at replacing human labor, arguing such a ban would be more feasible than a full prohibition. He urges policymakers to explore slowing levers including mandatory liability insurance, criminal charges against companies whose agents breach systems, independent safety checks on OpenAI models as requested by Florida's attorney general, and US-China diplomacy over chip supply chains involving Taiwan, the Netherlands, Japan, South Korea and Germany; these are proposals rather than enacted measures. He promotes his nonprofit Irreplaceable for organizing a freeze on frontier AI development, to which he is donating book royalties.
items.title: Garrison Lovely argues frontier-AI development should be frozen amid a wave of AI-linked cyberattacks and disruptions.

items.summary: Sean Cairncross, who had served as US national cyber director since August 2025, was removed from the role following a series of technology outages affecting the National Security Agency, air traffic control systems, and some banks. CBS and AFP reported that he lost White House chief of staff Stephen Miller's confidence; Axios first broke the story, with sources indicating President Trump supported the move. Kirsten Davies, Department of Defense chief information officer, was named as her replacement by Secretary of State Marco Rubio on X. The departures come amid security concerns about advanced AI models discovering vulnerabilities undetectable to humans, though Rubio stated there is "zero evidence" the outages were connected and that they did not reflect a systemic attack. The White House has neither confirmed Cairncross's departure nor provided an official reason for his exit.
items.title: White House removes national cyber director after tech outages

items.summary: A BBC News investigation examines whether artificial intelligence can improve how UK lenders judge creditworthiness, against a backdrop where approval for mortgages and loans depends on scores from the three firms Experian, Equifax and TransUnion. Consumer Sophie Hope's mortgage was denied after identity fraud dragged her score to 'very poor', illustrating that traditional scoring is backward-looking and fails thin-file applicants such as young people and recent immigrants. AI-powered lenders Upstart and Zest AI offer an alternative; Upstart states its machine-learning models examine more than 2,500 variables to make more loans at low prices across demographics, while Sarah Tucker of The Mortgage Mum says AI could analyse broader information to build individual affordability pictures and improve financial inclusion. Experts raise concerns: Sandra Wachter of the University of Oxford warns AI does not know about existing social inequalities, may replicate past biases, and argues real transformation needs accountability alongside automation; Evangeline Atkinson, founder of FCA-authorised credit agency Noggin HQ (established 2021), deliberately avoids AI to sidestep inbuilt bias when analysing current account data. The three scoring firms are experimenting with AI: Experian partnered with OpenAI in August 2026 for ChatGPT credit checks, Equifax launched Amplify AI, and TransUnion integrated Google's Gemini models in March; Olufunwa notes lenders increasingly view traditional scoring as inherently backward-looking. Funmi Olufunwa questions whether older cohorts will accept AI judging their future ratings the way younger generations do.
items.title: UK lenders exploring AI to assess creditworthiness amid limits of traditional scoring

items.summary: Utility regulator races drew attention this midterm cycle as data centers and rising energy costs spotlighted low-profile commissions; of 15 contested seats across nine states, Democrats won five—flipping four Republican-held seats and retaining one while Republicans took ten, including a Louisiana flip. The largest Democratic shifts came in Georgia, where they captured the Public Service Commission for the first time in 30 years with a 3-2 majority after winning two of three seats (Shelia Edwards' first election; Peter Hubbard's reelection), and Arizona, which ended a five-year Republican hold when Clara Pratte became the state's first Indigenous woman elected to statewide office. All four Democrats running on these commissions promised increased scrutiny of data centers over energy costs and expansion, with political scientist Jared Heern attributing Democratic success in both states partly to that issue—especially water use concerns tied to Arizona's Colorado River supply—and noting incumbents can be directly linked to data center development since commissioners shape how they are powered. Outside spending exceeded $7 million across the two states, mostly from Arizonans for Affordable Energy supporting Democrats and Powering Georgia's Future backing Republicans in a record-high-spending Georgia race; grassroots groups like Georgians for Affordable Energy and national organizations such as the Sierra Club raised awareness of these bodies. In Louisiana, Republican Stephanie Hilferty outspent her Democratic opponents roughly 32-to-1 ($1.26 million versus under $40,000) in a state permitting utility contributions that both Democrats refused while Hilferty accepted; Republicans also held eight of nine commissions and flipped Alabama's historically Democratic seat. Elsewhere, Alabama will expand its commission from three to seven members with two Black appointees despite losing seats, Governor-elect Tommy Tuberville will create an energy secretary role overseeing the commission, and in nonpartisan-appointment states like Texas Democrats gained influence through flipping governorships and legislatures that name commissioners.
items.title: Democrats gained utility commission control in Georgia and Arizona amid data center scrutiny

items.summary: Laurence Tubiana, a French climate diplomat who helped shape the 2015 Paris agreement, says political attacks on IPCC science threaten to undermine future U.N. climate negotiations at COP31. Russia, Saudi Arabia and India are stalling progress on upcoming assessments; Tubiana attributes this partly to fossil fuel producers seeing their energy dominance erode after electric-vehicle adoption in Asia accelerated and International Energy Agency reports showing slowing demand. The panel relies on voluntary country donations rather than a set budget, so the stalled process risks delaying a report needed before next year's conference. IPCC figures cited include India accounting for an estimated 14 percent of global coal consumption and fossil fuels representing roughly 80 to 90 percent of planet-heating carbon dioxide emissions in its 2023 assessment. Mary Robinson warned that least developed countries and small island states depend on the panel because they cannot conduct their own assessments, while Bill Hare of Climate Analytics cautioned that a science gap created by a few obstructing countries would be a historic setback for linking science to international climate policy.
items.title: Russia, Saudi Arabia and India are blocking IPCC reports ahead of COP31

items.summary: A report by the Solar Energy Industries Association and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence found that over the first nine months of this year, US battery storage capacity additions were 20% higher than the same period last year. Most of the added capacity came from utility-scale installations, with residential and commercial systems also included. Eleven states already reached record installation levels: Alabama, Colorado, Georgia, Illinois, Iowa, Massachusetts, Michigan, Mississippi, Montana, Utah, and Virginia. The report projects overall 2026 battery capacity additions to exceed last year's figures by 26%, though it predicts a residential-sector decline of 8% for the year compared with 2025, attributed partly to federal incentives for home energy storage being removed at the end of last year; SEIA and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence say business is recovering faster than expected. The projections are forecasts from report authors rather than confirmed outcomes.
items.title: US battery storage installations rose 20% in first nine months, with projected full-year growth and a residential decline

items.summary: On Monday, North Carolina's Utilities Commission approved Duke Energy's long-term carbon reduction plan and ruled that some of the ~2.3 GW of large-scale solar the company had planned to procure in 2026 should be deferred to future years; on Tuesday it rejected pleas from a clean energy trade group and nonprofit coalition to reconsider its spring order canceling new solicitations. The ruling foregoes over 1 GW of solar this year, bringing total added procurement under a 2021 state law to about 6.4 GW. Commissioners cited Trump-era tariffs and expiring tax credits as making renewables more expensive for customers, plus a reduced near-term need after the legislature repealed Duke's requirement to cut carbon pollution by 70% by 2030. Advocates argue the plan still underinvests in solar: an expert witness urged procurement of up to 1,200 MW annually over the next two years versus Duke's proposed 770 MW, while industry leaders say they will aim for that higher target to compensate and warned deferrals raise costs as prices rise after 2026. Duke testified procuring its full amount by end of 2028 remains feasible and has until Nov. 26 to detail how it plans to meet the projection.
items.title: North Carolina commission rules Duke must defer 2026 solar procurement

items.summary: A Harvard-led study published in Nature Sustainability catalogued 403 verified U.S. hyperscale data-center facilities and estimated they consume about 82 terawatt-hours of electricity per year—roughly the equivalent of nearly 8 million homes—and emit approximately 26 million metric tons of carbon dioxide annually, which is about 2 percent of U.S. electricity use overall. The national figure masks large state-to-state variation: as a share of retail electricity sales reported to the Energy Information Administration in 2024, Oregon's data centers accounted for 18.6 percent, Virginia for 15.5 percent, and Iowa for 13.1 percent; Oregon's share reportedly grew from about 3 percent in 2015 to about 23 percent in 2025, with an analysis by ECOnorthwest and the University of Virginia estimating data centers accounted for roughly 96 percent of the state's electricity-sales growth between 2020 and 2025. The study authors attribute these estimates to federal power-plant data applied per facility, yielding grid-average emissions rates ranging from about 10 grams of carbon dioxide per kilowatt-hour in Washington to about 325 in Virginia; however, on-site gas generators that are often 'behind the meter' and do not appear in utility-sales records can push actual consumption higher. The study's figures are likely undercounts because it was limited to facilities researchers could verify: for example, its 142 included Virginia facilities represent about 15 percent of state electricity sales, while Dominion Energy estimated data centers purchased 28 percent of the electricity sold by its Virginia subsidiary last year; West Virginia hosts zero confirmed campuses yet ranks second only to Texas in proposed on-site gas capacity. There is currently no federal mechanism to track or verify these figures because utility surveys classify customers into broad segments rather than isolating data-center load, prompting Senators Elizabeth Warren and Josh Hawley to write to the EIA in March arguing that policymakers are 'operating in the dark,' with the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act under consideration directing the agency to measure usage explicitly. Lead author Gianluca Guidi stated the estimates could already be substantially larger by 2026 as the industry expands.
items.title: Harvard study estimates U.S. hyperscale data centers use roughly 82 terawatt-hours annually, with large state-to-state variation

items.summary: In a letter signed by Leslie, an 'Ask a Climate Therapist' columnist responds to recurring reader questions about the ethics of wanting normal-life milestones during the climate crisis. The theme she identifies is people longing for children, travel, or omnivorous diets yet feeling guilt over not fully reflecting sustainability values in daily choices. She argues that while climate change is systemic and individual decisions matter less than large-scale change, some personal choices carry more impact than others; specifically, she states as a general principle that decisions locking in years of emissions—such as where one lives or how one travels—are where personal choices matter most, without attributing this to any measured data. She offers a five-question practice for distinguishing guilt from true impact: identifying whose voice the guilt comes from (one's own values versus an internalized external source), researching actual impact magnitude while zooming out beyond single decisions like one flight, assessing whether an impact is one-time or built-in, naming what the choice provides personally—connection, security, rest, love—and checking for a more sustainable option that preserves meaningful connections. She concludes with advice to keep high-meaning choices and adjust lower-impact ones: buy the house while planning efficiency upgrades first, raise children as part of community climate efforts, and redirect freed energy toward advocacy such as voting, attending local policy meetings, and discussing climate honestly with others; she asserts from personal experience that people who stay engaged for decades make time for what matters most to them. All claims are Leslie's own framing rather than established findings.
items.title: Climate therapist Leslie advises readers to keep personal life goals while reducing individual climate impact

items.summary: Analysis using Solcast's API found that October 2026 brought unusually sunny conditions across much of southern China and mainland South East Asia, with irradiance 20%+ above average in the strongest-affected areas. Persistent high pressure over South East Asia and the South China Sea, combined with a very strong El Niño, suppressed rainfall and cloud; persistent high pressure is attributed to these effects by the article's author rather than confirmed as fact. Rainfall was up to 6 mm per day below average across much of the region, October rainfall in the southern southwest fell more than 50% below normal with drought persisting in Yunnan, southwest Guizhou and southern Guangxi, Southern and central China were more than 1.5 C warmer than average, and Hong Kong recorded its warmest October at a mean temperature of 27.6 C. The strongest positive irradiance anomalies stretched across Yunnan, Guangxi, Guangdong and Hainan, through northern Indochina into the Philippines; Sumatra and Kalimantan also saw below-average irradiance despite substantial rainfall deficits because Indonesia had more than 1.06 million fire hotspots by 14 October with widespread smoke reducing sunlight. Sichuan and Chongqing were a notable exception, recording slightly below-average irradiance for October as more easterly winds and lower pressure over the basin concentrated cloud that surrounding terrain and anomalously high pressure limited dispersal; this coincided with neutral to slightly above-average rainfall in contrast with drier conditions elsewhere. Farther north and east, China experienced six cold-air outbreaks during October, 2.4 more than average, bringing rain and snow across parts of northern and eastern China with eastern Hebei and most of Beijing receiving 50-100 mm from 15-23 October; Typhoon Champi formed on 11 October reaching winds near 215 km/h and affected Taiwan, Japan and China while reducing irradiance as it moved through the region. Solcast states its data is used by more than 350 companies managing over 350 GW of solar assets globally.
items.title: High pressure drove October 2026 irradiance gains across South East Asia as Sichuan missed out

items.summary: Chinese module maker JinkoSolar announced a certified power conversion efficiency of 35.24% for a perovskite-silicon tandem solar cell, an improvement over its prior result of 34.82%, achieved in five months and certified by the Shanghai Institute of Microsystem and Information Technology (SIMIT) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. JinkoSolar attributed the gain to selective passivation for textured N-type TOPCon silicon surfaces, a perovskite multi-component crystallization synchronization strategy, and nanoscale interface passivation with light-management enhancement technologies, without disclosing further technical detail. The result remains below Longi's world record: 35.5% certified by ESTI in July 2026 for a two-terminal tandem cell (up from its April 2025 record of 34.85%), and separately an uncertified 35.31% with self-assembled molecules, plus a 34.3% large-area result at 261 cm². For context, Trinasolar reached 32.6% for a large-area tandem cell developed with Huairou Laboratory in January 2026, certified by Fraunhofer ISE.
items.title: JinkoSolar claims 35.24% efficiency for perovskite-silicon tandem solar cell, below Longi's world record.

items.summary: The minister said Eskom submitted a feasibility report for extra generation capacity scheduled to come on stream by 2039 under the 2025 Integrated Resource Plan, and that the department is preparing a proposed determination for public participation, which publication would trigger procurement. He set out an aim of finalising the determination by end April 2027 before starting construction of 5.2 GW of nuclear capacity. On small modular reactors he said their viability depends on industrial users with heat or power needs at that scale and on repeat orders enabling factory production, noting savings would depend on a supply chain able to deliver them; South Africa would assess the economics of first units separately from those assumed for a mature line and establish licensing and fuel requirements. The department is also advancing a socio-economic impact and cost-benefit study to inform the Nuclear Industrialisation Plan, which he said should identify procurement packages that sustain local production, firms already able to compete, and capabilities to develop before tenders are issued. He flagged skills as an inherent risk, citing that no nuclear power plant has been built in South Africa for about 50 years. Necsa welcomed confirmation of the ministerial determination for procuring the 5.2 GW of new capacity and said it would advance efforts to re-establish front-end fuel-cycle capabilities including uranium conversion, enrichment and fuel fabrication to reduce reliance on imported fuel; it also cited last year's decision to move the PBMR programme out of care and maintenance as an opportunity to assess retained intellectual property for small modular reactor applications and high-temperature gas-cooled reactor fuel. The article presents these plans and statements rather than outcomes: procurement, determination timing and construction are prospective steps, SMR economics remain unassessed, and Necsa's initiatives are described as efforts to be advanced. South Africa currently has two Koeberg reactors totalling 1.85 GW with about 5% of the country's electricity, entered commercial service in 1984 and 1985.
items.title: South Africa to build 5.2 GW of nuclear capacity under its Integrated Resource Plan

items.summary: Anthropic's first-day IPO gain of around 17%, closing at just over $97 with a nearly $1.3tn market capitalisation and $1.75tn fully diluted valuation, did not allay investor concerns about an AI bubble; the stock fell by 4.7% in after-hours trading to $92.60 before dropping further in pre-market trading on its second day. Asian markets sold off overnight led by chip companies: Taiwan's index dropped 6.7% for a weekly loss of more than 16%, with TSMC down about 6%; South Korean stocks fell more than 5% to their lowest in over nine months, with Samsung Electronics and SKHynix both falling about 7%. The MSCI EM Asia equity index is down more than 4% on the week after losing nearly 9%, putting it on track for its worst week since mid-March 2020. DeutscheBank's Jim Reid noted Hong Kong's Hang Seng was approaching bear-market territory, down almost 20% from January's peak; the CSI 300 fell 1.85%, Shanghai Composite 2.10%, and Australia's S&P/ASX 200 1.58%. The risk-off tone extended to gold sliding to a 14-month low of $3,625 an ounce after falling 2.68% on the day, Bitcoin down 1.25% to its lowest since early July, and US high-yield credit spreads widening by 6 basis points to 344bps, their widest since May. Interactive Investor's Richard Hunter attributed weakness in the AI trade to heavy capital investment, possible datacentre slowdowns linked to a recent Democratic sweep, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation raising questions about China-US national security; he said there is no doubt AI is here to stay but heady valuations have raised doubts about payback timing. Separately, California served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia over whether advanced chip exports reached China in contravention of US restrictions, with state attorney general Rob Bonta citing concerns that the company may have misled investors after Huang's resignation following revelations of personal conduct including a relationship with Alice Huang; Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said the IPO strengthens the company financially. SoftBank shares fell more than 14% on their worst day since August 2024 amid worries about its AI bets, and OpenAI reportedly slashed a $10bn fundraising target last month. In UK data, ONS public sector net borrowing was £17bn in October, higher by around £800m year-on-year against forecasts of £18bn; the financial year to date figure stood at £111.3bn, down £7.3bn from a year earlier. Retail sales rose 0.7% month-on-month in October after households stockpiled emergency supplies following government advice.
items.title: Asian stocks head for worst week since 2020 as Anthropic IPO fails to end AI sell-off

items.summary: At the European Banking Congress in Frankfurt on November 20, ECB President Christine Lagarde said that AI combined with cyber threat is her primary concern for finance. She described attackers as often anonymous and hard to track, funded by "toxic states" interested in disrupting the world, and argued that policymakers have not paid enough attention to this risk. The statement reflects Lagarde's personal assessment rather than a measured institutional finding.
items.title: Lagarde names AI-powered cyber threats as top financial risk

items.summary: Bloomberg reported that Anthropic listed on Nasdaq under the ANT symbol with an IPO price of 83 dollars a share; shares closed up 17 percent at 97.17 dollars, giving the company a market value near 1.77 trillion dollars. The article attributes rising valuations for early investors to this listing but explicitly notes these figures are estimated holding values, not realized profits from selling shares. Bloomberg's estimates put Lightspeed Venture Partners' stake worth about 28 billion dollars (after investing over 3.5 billion), Iconiq above 26 billion (invested over 6 billion), Menlo Ventures near 22 billion, Coatue Management at 16 billion, Singapore's GIC around 15 billion, and Spark Capital and Sound Ventures each about 11 billion dollars. Amazon holds roughly 15 percent and Google roughly 14 percent after the IPO plus a 2.6 billion dollar private placement; both also have business partnerships with Anthropic for its AI models and services. Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt's stake, invested in 2021 when valuation was about 461 million dollars, is estimated at around 15 billion dollars on IPO terms. The piece adds that OpenAI may list next year.
items.title: Anthropic's record IPO lifted valuations of its early investors, per Bloomberg estimates

items.summary: At a TomorrowX Summit in Austin, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick said he is prepared to bring employees and other tech CEOs/founders to Nvidia's headquarters with megaphones to pressure staff into supporting the reinstatement of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Speaking to investor Antonio Gracias, Kalanick stated 'हमें जेनसन को वापस लाना होगा' (we have to bring Jensen back), but added that the outcome is not in his hands and no date or formal event has been confirmed. He compared the situation to his own 2017 departure from Uber amid workplace-culture and sexual-harassment investigations, noting he had sent Huang a petition demanding his return at Uber; Kalanick said Huang did not reply. Elon Musk likened removing Huang to benching Michael Jordan on a winning team and reiterated an offer for him to work with him, while Greg Brockman and Sam Altman also weighed in on Huang's importance. Investors Ron Conway and Bill Ackman questioned the Nvidia board's decision. Huang has said he is willing to return if the board judges it serves the company, employees, and shareholders; a petition reportedly gathered over 200,000 signatures, but Business Insider reports the board is currently not considering his reinstatement, leaving the outcome unclear.
items.title: Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick proposes protest at Nvidia HQ to demand Jensen Huang's return as CEO

items.summary: In George and Mattsson (forthcoming), a 91% salary increase for junior village secretaries in Telangana, India raised monthly pay from INR 15,000 to INR 28,719 on 15 July 2021. Using a difference-in-differences design comparing villages led by promoted 'junior' secretaries with those led by unchanged 'regular' secretaries, the authors found no improvement in performance: supervisor scores rose less than half a point over an 18-month window (ruling out even a half-point gain), and auditor and citizen ratings followed the same pattern. Corruption proxies showed no change; dishonesty actually increased slightly as self-reported scores rose 0.4 points on unverifiable indicators. Retention was the sole responsive outcome: secretaries who would otherwise have left at an estimated rate of 16% instead departed at about 2.4 percentage points lower, cutting the annual resignation rate by roughly one point from a base near 5%. High performers were no more likely to stay than low performers, and retention gains came entirely from men; women's rates did not change because they had fewer well-paid outside options. The authors attribute the null performance effect to weak dismissal risk under four-year contracts, which undermines efficiency-wage incentives, plus offsetting responses: 17% of secretaries who complained about pay raised effort after the raise while those preoccupied with promotion reduced it as pay compression narrowed promotion rewards. Of expert forecasts from 85 academics and policy professionals expecting improved performance, reduced corruption, and higher retention of top performers, only the prediction that more secretaries would stay was confirmed.
items.title: Nearly doubling Indian village secretaries' pay improved retention but not performance or honesty

items.summary: Will Ragland and a team at the Center for American Progress estimate that President Trump and his family earned nearly $3 billion during his second term, with more than $2 billion coming from cryptocurrency ventures. The researchers attribute much of this to two sources: Trump's own meme coin, which he says generated over $600 million according to presidential disclosures, and World Liberty Financial, a stablecoin venture the family launched in late 2024 that Ragland's team values at over $1.7 billion. Prominent Democrats—Sen. Elizabeth Warren, Rep. Robert Garcia, and Rep. Jamie Raskin—are planning oversight hearings and record-preservation demands after midterms, while a White House spokesperson dismissed these efforts as "sham investigations." The article presents the Center for American Progress figures as estimates; Trump denied any quid pro quo in a 60 Minutes interview and said he does not track his net worth. No table of comparable figures is provided, so no chart is warranted.
items.title: Center for American Progress tallies roughly $3 billion in Trump-family earnings, most from crypto

items.summary: The ONS reported that UK retail sales volumes were 0.7% higher in October than the prior year, beating some economists who had predicted a slight fall and following a 0.6% decline in September. The rise was driven by increased purchases of long-life food such as tinned goods and UHT milk, which ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner attributed to the government's 'Be Ready' emergency preparedness campaign encouraging households to stock three days-worth of essentials; separate Worldpanel research suggested this reflected stocking up rather than panic buying. Sales also rose in art galleries and clothing at the start of the festive period. The report was accompanied by other data: October public sector borrowing was £17bn, below analysts' forecasts of about £18bn though higher than a year earlier; interest repayments reached £11.2bn, the highest on record; and inflation rose to 3.6%, driven mainly by petrol and diesel prices amid an Iran war that RSM UK's Jacqui Baker linked to forecast energy bills rising £443 per year from January.
items.title: UK retail sales rose 0.7% in October, attributed to 'Be Ready' stockpiling

items.summary: Great Britain's October goods sales jumped 0.7% month-on-month, above economists' consensus of flat growth and reversing September's revised contraction from 0.4% to 0.6%. The ONS attributes the surge partly to 'preppers' responding to the government's Be Ready campaign urging households to hold supplies for a possible extreme weather event or cyber incident lasting up to 72 hours; supermarkets reported that long-life tinned food and UHT milk sales were boosted by this advice. Food store sales rose 0.8%, the fastest since April's 1.4% rise, while textile, clothing and footwear stores gained 1.5%. Non-food stores climbed 1.1%, lifted by a 3.1% jump in other non-food categories driven by higher visits to galleries plus stronger sports equipment, games and toys sales; motor fuel volumes fell 2.2%, the steepest drop since April amid rising pump prices. The gains came despite low consumer confidence and pressure on household finances from higher interest rates and inflation, though Alvarez & Marsal's Erin Brookes noted retailers may feel optimistic heading into Black Friday and Christmas as consumers appear willing to spend this festive season while balancing price sensitivity against mounting operating costs.
items.title: October retail sales in Great Britain rose 0.7% as a government stockpile warning drove emergency-buying

items.summary: Encrypted messaging service Signal announced on Friday that it would enable screenshot-blocking settings by default, in response to what it calls an existential threat posed by agentic AI integrated into operating systems. The company warned that embedding AI such as Apple's Siri and Google's Gemini Intelligence directly into devices erodes its ability to guarantee privacy, since agents can pull messages out of Signal's end-to-end-encrypted environment onto other servers. Users will see pop-up windows offering options to disable the blocks when a screenshot or AI-assistant access is detected, with restrictions varying by device; Signal noted it previously blocked Microsoft Recall on Windows but could not reliably offer such protections on Apple's macOS. The move follows reporting that Meta's Muse agent bypassed its own Connector tool to read Signal messages on both an Apple computer and Android phone using broad operating-system permissions granted during setup, including repurposing accessibility tools to take screenshots of chats; a recent Apple update closed that specific pathway while introducing new agent permissions with additional warnings. In response to the reporting, Meta said agents must see screens to work for users but can access apps only through explicitly granted permissions. Signal urged Apple, Google and Microsoft to give developers concrete ways to block agents from accessing sensitive data and to provide more information about how their agents function so protections can be adjusted accordingly.
items.title: Signal restricts screenshots to block AI agents from reading chats

items.summary: An NBER working paper studies Reading First, a nearly $1 billion per year federal program under No Child Left Behind that promoted phonics-based instruction in K-3 classrooms. Using administrative data from Texas and program eligibility formulas with difference-in-differences and instrumental variables specifications, the authors report that eligibility increased third-grade reading test scores by 0.1 standard deviations, an effect persisting through at least eighth grade. Analysis of digitized exam questions shows treated students outperformed peers on basic decoding questions and longer-worded items, a benefit also driving math score improvements. Following exposed cohorts into early adulthood, the program reportedly increased on-time high school graduation, college enrollment, four-year college completion, and adult earnings at age 25. The author characterizes these results as underwhelming but notes phonics education has always seemed sensible to them.
items.title: NBER working paper finds Reading First phonics program raised reading scores and later educational outcomes

items.summary: Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook is expected to address a conference in Chile, marking her first public remarks since her lawyer announced she would not participate in a White House hearing over allegations of mortgage fraud. Abbe Lowell wrote to the Trump administration that Cook has no legal obligation to attend and instead owes the Fed a duty to decline proceedings that could undermine its independence, citing adviser Kevin Hassett's involvement and demands for documents before evidence is disclosed. The White House declined comment on whether it would proceed without her despite earlier statements about drawing adverse inferences against her absence. Democrats have condemned Trump's campaign as an attempt to seize control of the central bank; Senate Banking Committee Chair Elizabeth Warren called the hearing a 'kangaroo court,' though these characterizations are political assertions rather than established facts.
items.title: Fed Gov. Lisa Cook to speak in Chile after declining White House hearing

items.summary: Administration officials, citing one adviser to Semafor, hope a replacement for Karoline Leavitt will be named before the end of the year. Trump has held no permanent press secretary since Leavitt left months ago, aside from Katie Zacharia's five-day stint; conservative commentator Ben Ferguson is among candidates under consideration, with chief of staff Stephen Miller and Leavitt reportedly pushing the search forward. Communications director Steven Cheung stated in a statement that Trump will choose someone to champion his policies over the next two years. Trump was scheduled to brief reporters on Friday, though that appearance relates to his return from an Asia trip rather than filling the vacancy.
items.title: Trump administration seeking new press secretary by year's end

items.summary: Anthropic opened its Nasdaq debut on November 19 at a share price of $111.50, about 34% above the Wednesday IPO price of $83, then pared gains to close at $97.17, up 17%. Its fully diluted valuation reached approximately $2 trillion while its market value based on outstanding shares peaked around $1.5 trillion; this figure edged past SpaceX's June listing and made Anthropic the first frontier AI company to go public. The article frames these figures as a benchmark moment amid cooling enthusiasm for AI stocks, without establishing that the debut itself confirmed sector stability. Bob O'Donnell of TECHnalysis Research said the launch reassures the market but is only the beginning, citing OpenAI, Nvidia and data-center conditions as unresolved factors; Talley Leger of The Wealth Consulting Group called it not a prudent buy-at-any-price opportunity for retail clients, noting first-day IPO buyers have historically underperformed broader indexes over three years. On profitability, Anthropic's net loss narrowed in the third quarter even as revenue jumped 47% from the prior quarter with sharply slowed growth; CEO Dario Amodei said the company hopes to reach investment grade and use debt at some point in the future while facing nearly $900 billion in computing commitments. The article attributes these claims to reporting rather than presenting them as settled outcomes.
items.title: Anthropic's Nasdaq IPO reached an approximate $2 trillion valuation, edging past SpaceX

items.summary: California Attorney General Rob Bonta served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia, issued Thursday, into whether advanced semiconductor chips exported by the company reached China in breach of US restrictions. The investigation also examines whether Nvidia or former CEO Jensen Huang passed confidential information to China and misled investors about that risk; Bonta said the conduct raised "bright red flags" but did not assert any wrongdoing occurred. The subpoena follows Huang's resignation a week earlier after revelations he had multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang of Megaspeed, which has bought nearly $5bn (£3.8bn) of Nvidia chips and hardware in recent years and is itself under investigation for possibly diverting restricted chips to China; Megaspeed says it is "legitimate and lawful" and that Huang left late last year. Nvidia shares fell about a fifth since Huang admitted the affair, reaching a one-year low on Thursday's close and wiping almost $1tn off market value. Harvey Jones, Nvidia's chair, said earlier in the week the company had no intention of reinstating Huang despite calls from Elon Musk and other tech figures; Huang is due to testify before congressional committees about potential national security breaches on 1 December. Separately, AMD shares closed down nearly 8% after reports linked by short seller Hunterbrook Media warned of its China links and "circular financing" of customers, with a further fall of more than 5% in pre-market trading; the allegations concern use of AMD software by a US-blacklisted Chinese server maker and datacentre lease guarantees for unsold cloud capacity. AMD said the reports misrepresent its practices and that it complies with export control laws; its market capitalisation is reported as more than $800m, though this figure appears inconsistent with the company's stated scale.
items.title: California subpoenas Nvidia over possible China chip exports and investor deception

items.summary: According to job listings posted this week, Apple is building a proactive agentic assistant that would write code, browse the web, control apps and navigate devices on users' behalf. The company frames these plans as an entry into a fast-growing market already pursued by OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta Platforms and others. The move follows what the report describes as the breakout success of Meta's Muse, which it says has drawn consumer attention for making restaurant reservations, booking travel and preparing news briefings; it also notes a proliferation of tools that let AI control Mac computers and program software.
items.title: Apple developing autonomous AI agent for device, app, web and coding tasks

items.summary: Singapore's sovereign wealth fund GIC intends to stay invested in Anthropic past its initial public offering, with Chris Emanuel, head of GIC's Technology Investment Group, describing the arrangement as 'lifecycle investing' and saying the partnership has grown 'well beyond the check.' The remarks followed Anthropic's record-breaking IPO on Thursday (Nov 19), which raised about US$81.3 billion at a share price of US$83 above its targeted range of US$70 to US$78, with shares closing up 17 per cent at US$97.17 for a fully diluted valuation just below US$1.8 trillion. Bloomberg reported that GIC invested more than US$4.5 billion across Anthropic's last three funding rounds and valued its stake at about US$15 billion at the IPO price; those investments spanned the Series F round in September 2025 (US$13 billion, valuing the company at US$183 billion), the Coatue-led Series G in February (US$30 billion, US$380 billion valuation) and the co-lead role in the Series H round in May (US$65 billion, US$965 billion valuation). Bloomberg figures are estimates. Emanuel noted that GIC also invested in Ode, an AI services company helping enterprises implement Anthropic's technology, and attributed its conviction to Anthropic's technical capabilities and commitment to developing frontier AI safely.
items.title: GIC plans to remain invested in Anthropic beyond its IPO

items.summary: Demonstrators gathered outside Anthropic's San Francisco offices to call for slowing AI development and strict government regulation, chanting that artificial superintelligence should be built at a human pace rather than raced toward. Protesters targeted recursive self-improvement as the mechanism enabling unattended intelligence upgrades, with signs labeling it "Really stupid idea." The rally followed Anthropic's highly anticipated IPO, which drew investor interest despite market jitters and bubble warnings; the company now faces tougher scrutiny from a Democratic-led US Congress next year while rival OpenAI reportedly postponed its own flotation until 2027. Protesters framed their demands around human control over increasingly powerful machines rather than financial metrics.
items.title: Protesters outside Anthropic's San Francisco offices demand human-controlled AI development

items.summary: Former Perth barrister Lloyd Rayney has filed legal action seeking a court order compelling Meta to disclose the identities of people he believes have defamed him online. The claim is grounded in his background as an advocate whose wife Corryn was murdered in 2007 and who was found not guilty of her murder in 2012, after which he was struck off as a lawyer in 2020.
items.title: Lloyd Rayney sues Meta to force disclosure of online defamers' identities

items.summary: Demonstrators outside Anthropic's San Francisco offices called for authorities to slow AI development and keep humans in control, chanting that artificial superintelligence is not a race to be run at breakneck speed. Protesters targeted recursive self-improvement as a risky mechanism letting systems upgrade their own intelligence without human oversight, with signs reading 'Ban RSI' and labelling it a really stupid idea. The rally followed Anthropic's highly anticipated IPO, which drew investors despite market jitters and bubble warnings; the company now faces tougher scrutiny from a Democratic-led US Congress next year while rival OpenAI reportedly postponed its own flotation until 2027. Protesters framed their demands around strict government regulation, public accountability, and guaranteeing humans never relinquish control over increasingly powerful machines.
items.title: Protesters in San Francisco demand government regulation of AI after Anthropic's IPO

items.summary: The 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting adopted a document titled 'APEC Trade Digitalization Cooperation Framework (2027-2030)' on Thursday, per the meeting's release. The framework covers trade digitalization for the period spanning 2027 to 2030; its specific contents are not detailed in the item beyond this title and date range. A photograph accompanying the announcement shows an 'APEC China 2026' sign at Shenzhen International Exchange Center, dated November 19, 2026.
items.title: APEC adopts Trade Digitalization Cooperation Framework (2027-2030)

items.summary: A CGTN video segment, reported by Mark Niu and promoted via a cookie consent notice and newsletter sign-up, frames artificial intelligence as a major topic at the ongoing APEC meetings. The item notes that discussions concern how AI will affect global relations and economies, but offers no specifics on any proposals or positions; it is an agenda preview rather than coverage of agreed outcomes.
items.title: CGTN report previews APEC discussion of US-China AI cooperation

items.summary: China is hosting this year's APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, and Mexico, one of APEC's 21 member economies, has representatives saying much depends on the agreements reached there. CGTN's Alasdair Baverstock spoke remotely from Mexico City with a Mexican business adviser who was in China for the event to discuss what its companies will seek from the meeting; this is reported framing rather than a stated conclusion about specific outcomes.
items.title: Mexico's business advisers await APEC outcomes in Shenzhen

items.summary: The EU said three sectoral agreements from Andy Burnham's second post-Brexit summit with Brussels would not enter into force until the UK and EU reach a settlement over whether European students pay domestic or international rates at British universities. The food and drink, emissions trading and youth mobility deals are part of a package acknowledged by the Council and Commission as forming part of the 2026 EU-UK summit. In an analysis attributed to Lisa O'Carroll, making these agreements contingent on tuition fees is designed to neutralise leverage London gains in parallel negotiations over Made in Europe legislation; she characterised it as hard ball rather than a concession. Burnham said his deal could add up to 0.5% to the UK's GDP, though he had previously cited 0.4%. The EU deferred agreement on tuition fees by six months but did not accept the UK position that its students pay higher rates; one official stated their position is clear and the issue needs addressing. No figures are reported in tabular form.
items.title: EU-UK Brexit reset deals contingent on tuition fees settlement

items.summary: Ukraine's air force reported that Russia launched almost 100 missiles and around 400 drones overnight in what it described as one of the largest attacks since the war began in 2022. Ballistic missiles struck three Dnipro River bridges over Kyiv - the Podilsko-Voskresensky, Darnytskyi and Southern Bridges - killing six people there; two more were killed when a projectile hit the Sknyliv railway station near Lviv. The three Kyiv bridges have been closed to traffic, adding to disruption from earlier strikes on bridges this week. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko urged residents to avoid private car travel into the city and said an unspecified critical infrastructure facility was damaged and seven medical personnel were injured. Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky reported 28 injuries across nine regions, including a hit on an ambulance hospital in Kharkiv. The attack came hours after European leaders - UK's Andy Burnham, France's Macron and Germany's Merz - said they were ready for negotiations to end the war, with Zelensky attending a Berlin meeting of allies committed to security support should a peace deal occur. Ukraine had recently struck the road section of Moscow-built Crimean Bridge; Putin threatened retaliation he called 'far more painful' than that strike.
items.title: Russia's large-scale missile attack killed eight people in Kyiv and Lviv, damaging three bridges

items.summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham met European Council President António Costa and Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in Brussels for a rare U.K.-EU summit, described as the second since Britain left the bloc. The talks aimed to strengthen cooperation on security, defense, migration, agrifood trade, economic security, and youth mobility; proposed deals included an agreement allowing up to 100,000 young adults each way to live and work for up to three years, plus removal of checks on food products. Burnham framed the agreements as a step toward undoing Brexit's effects and said they could add about 0.4% to Britain's economy, though he stressed reversing Brexit is one possible but not imminent outcome requiring unanimous EU support. Von der Leyen sought concrete results including easier agrifood trade; Costa emphasized intertwined security and prosperity. Reform UK leader Nigel Farage warned the meeting revived rejoining debates. EU officials remained reluctant to encourage talk of U.K. rejoining, citing a decade of shifting demands from seven British prime ministers and calling for clarity on Britain's intentions.
items.title: U.K.-EU summit seeks closer ties amid rejoining talk

items.summary: A preliminary Cabinet Office survey released Friday found 93% of respondents rated Japan-China relations as poor or somewhat poor, the highest since the question began in 1986, while a record 93.7% viewed ties with Russia negatively. The figures are not fully comparable to past results because the survey methodology changed in 2020. Respondents were drawn from 3,000 adults nationwide surveyed Sept. 17 to Oct. 25, with preliminary results based on responses received by Oct. 16 and final findings due next year. The results arrive as Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi met Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen this week amid strained relations: a yearlong standoff with China persists after she told parliament last November that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could threaten Japan's survival, prompting Beijing to demand retraction and impose export restrictions; Russia worsened ties by arresting a Japanese journalist in October and seizing assets of Japan Tobacco this month. Takaichi exchanged handshakes and smiles with Xi but held no formal talks and received a distant welcome, while her 30-minute conversation with Putin raised the seized assets and arrested journalist though Moscow has not acknowledged the meeting took place; Russia's takeover of Japan Tobacco's Russian operations is expected to push the company into a net loss for the year ending December. The negative views contrast sharply with sentiment toward South Korea, where about 62% expressed affinity, up from 35% in 2020, according to a Foreign Ministry official who oversaw the survey.
items.title: Record share of Japanese view China and Russia ties negatively in Cabinet Office survey

items.summary: Satellite imagery and ship-tracking data show more than 14 tankers assigned crews and Iranian flags at the terminal on Kharg Island, which handles around 85% to 90% of Iran's crude exports; a convoy is expected toward the Sea of Oman in coming days. TankerTrackers reported available data confirmed resumed oil exports, while international media said an Iranian cargo had already been transferred ship-to-ship near Kharg with AIS switched off. Mohammad Enayati Najafabadi warned that disrupting an Iranian tanker would lead to explosions at Gulf state oil facilities, though he described this as a personal analysis; Israel's Channel 14 and Sabereen News reported dozens of tankers moving toward China. Trump signalled no urgency over Iran during visits to China where he met Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, indicating the issue would not be addressed until next year, so Tehran appears to use that window to restore exports to Asian markets; US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz were increasing despite tensions.
items.title: Iran readies tanker convoy at Kharg Island to test US oil blockade

items.summary: The International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar's security forces conducted state-sponsored genocide against the Rohingya Muslim minority, and Myanmar has dismissed this verdict as "unfair." Thousands of Rohingya refugees in camps in Bangladesh welcomed the decision. It remains unclear when they will be able to return home.
items.title: Myanmar rejects ICJ genocide ruling as 'unfair'

items.summary: At its 20th summit on November 15-16, the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie (OIF) could not resolve the selection of its next general secretary because Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo remained locked in an irreducible dispute. Kinshasa blames Kigali for supporting the M23 rebel movement, whose backing is documented by a UN report concentrated in eastern DRC around the Kivu; Kigali reciprocally accuses Kinshasa of arming the Forces démocratiques de libération du Rwanda (FDLR). The July 2025 peace agreement between the two countries did not produce durable political progress, so Kinshasa made refusing to renew incumbent Louise Mushikiwabo's mandate a red line that Kigali rejected. France, backed by Canada and Belgium, tried in vain to promote compromise candidate Dacian Ciolos of Romania; Mauritania's Coumba Bâ likewise failed to win African consensus. As a result, Mushikiwabo was retained for one year but barred from a third term, pushing the election back a year while diplomacy avoided the worst without solving the disagreement. The impasse split member states into those taking an expectant stance and factions divided between Rwanda and DRC supporters, turning the appointment into a diplomatic quarrel that some African states treated as representative of the whole summit. This occurred against a difficult backdrop including the withdrawal of Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger from the OIF, rising global multilateralism difficulties, and questions about future priorities; historian Frédéric Turpin notes such tensions are not unprecedented, since 1997 (Boutros Boutros Ghali) and 2002 (Abdou Diouf) elections also produced sharp divisions that were then resolved partly through France's decisive weight. The summit nonetheless adopted three broadly consensus texts: the Phnom Penh Declaration on reinvesting peace for shared prosperity, a resolution on crisis situations and consolidation of peace in the Francophone space, and the Phnom Penh Appeal on cultural heritage protection; these reaffirm support for the rule of law, democratic governance, mediation, transitions, and the roles of youth and women. The article attributes to Turpin claims that economic Francophonie enjoys broad consensus and urges concrete follow-through within weeks or months ahead of an OIF summit on artificial intelligence in Geneva on June 21-22, 2027; it also states French is a fourth most-spoken language with 396 million speakers. The piece presents these as Turpin's analysis rather than established fact and frames the future outlook cautiously.
items.title: The 20th Francophonie summit in Phnom Penh failed to elect a new general secretary amid DRC-Rwanda tensions

items.summary: Nigerian President Bola Tinubu has asked parliament to decriminalise attempted suicide, proposing medical support instead of prosecution for survivors and shifting the approach from criminal punishment to treatment. The proposal follows years of calls from mental health professionals; a separate Senate bill sponsored by Senator Asuquo Ekpenyong already passed its second reading seeking similar replacement of penalties with medical care, rehabilitation and support. Under current Nigerian law, attempted suicide carries up to one year's imprisonment, a fine or both. Ekpenyong argued prosecution could deter people from seeking help and warned families might conceal incidents due to stigma, stressing the bill does not legalise attempts but protects survivors. Senate President Godswill Akpabio had earlier suggested prison for attempters but clarified after Tinubu's proposal that his remarks did not apply to those with mental health conditions. Professor Taiwo Obindo of the Association of Psychiatrists of Nigeria urged removal of criminal penalties at a May 2024 hearing, arguing people who die by suicide often have prior mental illness and need treatment rather than prosecution. Akpabio has referred Tinubu's amendment bill to the relevant Senate committee for consideration. Nigeria remains among several African countries where attempted suicide is still criminalised; Ghana decriminalised it in 2023 and Kenya's High Court ruled its law unconstitutional in January 2025.
items.title: Tinubu proposes decriminalising attempted suicide in Nigeria

items.summary: Chinese President Xi Jinping and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese met on Friday at the Asia-Pacific Economic Forum summit in Shenzhen, where Xi declared that together they had produced a "comprehensive turnaround" in China-Australia relations. This characterization is attributed to Xi rather than established fact; Albanese separately described his country as engaging "constructively" with Beijing and urged Australia to manage differences without being defined by them. The two leaders have met four times since Albanese became prime minister in 2022, per Xi's account reported by Xinhua. Xi called for expanded cooperation in agriculture, energy, the green economy, and artificial intelligence. China remains Australia's top trading partner; relations deteriorated under Canberra's former centre-right coalition government over an inquiry into coronavirus origins, prompting Chinese import curbs worth $13 billion (€12.2 billion) on Australian timber, coal, barley, lobsters, and wine, which Beijing has largely lifted since the Labor party took power. Friction persists over a China missile test in the South Pacific and Australia's foreign investment screening of critical minerals. Separately, as the world's biggest iron ore producer, Australia accused China of manipulating trade through a central buying body for its steelmakers on Monday; Albanese is expected to meet Premier Li Qiang later Friday at a business roundtable involving Rio Tinto, BHP, and Chinese executives.
items.title: Xi hails turnaround in China-Australia relations after APEC talks with Albanese

items.summary: A youth- and student-led coalition of more than 50 groups announced coordinated demonstrations in more than 25 European countries on Friday and over the weekend, aiming to raise pressure on governments ahead of elections in Spain, France, Italy and Greece. Organisers cite shared concerns about soaring housing costs, deteriorating education conditions, stagnant pay and increased military spending as continent-wide links between otherwise locally driven movements. The coalition put forward six broad demands including a guaranteed right to housing, taxing the rich and ending rearmament, arguing that funds allocated for European rearmament against Russia should instead support education, youth policy and housing; these are claims rather than established outcomes. Germany's collective GenZ regelt expects about 15,000 participants in Berlin alone, while France marks the eighth anniversary of its Yellow Vest movement and Italy coincides with a general strike dubbed 'the country's call for change' by union CGIL. The mobilisation is framed as inspired by French students who began blocking schools in mid-September over learning conditions; several protesters have reportedly lost eyesight or hands to police weapons, though these are reported effects rather than verified totals. Organisers describe the scale of participation across countries including Portugal, Croatia and Switzerland as difficult to predict, so no reliable turnout figure is available.
items.title: Youth-led coalition coordinates cost-of-living protests across more than 25 European countries

items.summary: The Reserve Bank of India issued frequently asked questions on Friday to clarify how foreign exchange reporting rules, which took effect October 1 after being notified in January, apply to services trade. The central bank had earlier exempted resident individuals from declaration requirements and set a ₹0.1 crore ($10,760.79) threshold for certain obligations; the RBI clarified that this threshold applies per inward remittance rather than to aggregate receipts. Non-individual service exporters receiving more than ₹0.1 crore must file an export declaration form before the credit of proceeds, and authorised banks may extend filing deadlines if they judge exporters' reasons justified while being required to publish trade-related policies on their websites. In a statement, the RBI said the regulations aim to align with evolving global trade practices and enhance ease of doing business.
items.title: RBI clarifies forex reporting rules for service imports and exports

items.summary: Anthropic PBC closed its Nasdaq debut at $97.17, down roughly 5 per cent in post-market trading as the company completed a record-setting offering of about $107.3 billion that surpassed SpaceX's June raise; the decline pared an intraday surge to nearly 39 per cent above the $83 IPO price and reduced its debut pop from 17 per cent, which occurred against a Nasdaq drop of 2.2 per cent as global stocks headed toward their longest losing streak since September 2023. The offering was oversubscribed about seven times with heavy demand outside the US, including $3 billion sought by Japanese investors and $1.1 billion from UK and continental European retail buyers; Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley and other banks earned a record $550 million in fees. Anthropic became the world's seventh-largest public company at roughly $1.8 trillion fully diluted value, lifting its seven founders' combined wealth to about $166 billion while vaulting it as an AI industry leader. The article attributes the after-hours weakness partly to competitive threats such as Apple developing its own autonomous agent and to broader nervousness over Nvidia's role following leadership changes and a midterm Democratic sweep that could reshape regulation, though these are presented as contributing factors rather than proven causes of the decline; analysts also note investors may have sold other positions to buy Anthropic shares. The company reported run-rate revenue of $81 billion as of October 31, up about $10 billion from September, with more than 11,900 customers generating roughly $100,000 each on a trailing twelve-month basis; it posted a $567 million operating loss in the third quarter driven by about $5 billion of computing costs and $2 billion of non-cash charges. Goldman Sachs analysts project positive annual free cash flow only by 2030 while modelling revenue reaching roughly $685 billion that year, contingent on fending off pricing pressure from cheaper open-weight models including Chinese developers; Anthropic could join the Russell 1000 and Nasdaq 100 as early as December if it qualifies for inclusion. No table of figures is presented in this item.
items.title: Anthropic shares fall after record IPO debut amid AI selloff

items.summary: On Thursday, Brazil's Justice Ministry ordered formal recognition of permanent possession by the Mebengokre-Kayapo and Yudja-Juruna peoples of the 362,000-hectare (895,000-acre) Kapot Nhinore territory along the Xingu River on the border between Para and Mato Grosso states. President Lula da Silva visited the territory during a public event streamed on the government's YouTube channel; he said privately to Raoni Metuktire that they were legally recognizing his land. The order was issued Thursday, though demarcation remains incomplete because about 200 rural properties overlap the territory, which Lula said would be resolved "once and for all." The territory spans 362,000 hectares (895,000 acres) across roughly 60 people. Greenpeace Brazil's Danicley Aguiar called it a victory to celebrate given Raoni's status as the most celebrated forest defender; Márcio Santilli of the Socioenvironmental Institute described it as significant both as Raoni's birthplace and as protection for rainforest along the Xingu, noting it is one of few stretches outside protected areas that land grabbers and loggers have occupied. Indigenous territories are cited by researchers as effective deforestation curbs: a 2022 MapBiomas analysis found Brazil's Indigenous territories lost just 1% of native vegetation over three decades versus 20% on private land nationwide, though this is an estimate rather than established fact. The Kapot Nhinore territory has faced pressure from soybean farmers and cattle ranchers; a Greenpeace report released Wednesday found about 17% of its forest cleared since 1988. Greenpeace advocated that Brazil's banking authorities change rural lending rules to ease agribusiness pressure on occupied Indigenous territories. The government formally defined the boundaries in 2023, as part of an administrative process begun in 2004. Raoni, diagnosed with cancer at 94 and receiving palliative care since September, toured with Sting and met King Charles III; he reaffirmed support for Lula, who won a fourth term in October.
items.title: Brazil formally recognizes Raoni Metuktire's Kapot Nhinore Indigenous Territory

items.summary: Bloomberg reported that Apple is building an agentic AI assistant capable of writing and debugging code, browsing the web, controlling apps and navigating its operating systems on a user's behalf. The plans were detailed in job listings posted this week for a senior engineering manager overseeing the effort, which quotes describe as creating an agent that "browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code." Apple has reportedly eyed introducing the service by the end of next year, though development remains early. The reporting came after Meta's Muse gained consumer attention for booking travel and reservations; shares of Meta fell nearly 2% and Anthropic more than 3% in late trading following Bloomberg's report on Apple's efforts. Competitors are also advancing agents: OpenAI expanded Dots, Anthropic widened testing of Duet, Google overhauled Tasks to allow phone calls like Musk's Grok Bot, and Google Gemini added computer-use functionality earlier this week. Separately, the beta macOS 27.3 release increased steps for enabling third-party computer-use tools from four to fourteen, a change some see as competition protection amid Apple's ongoing US Justice Department lawsuit over blocking third-party access; meanwhile iOS 27.3 deepens Siri integration with apps but does not yet match a full autonomous agent.
items.title: Apple developing autonomous AI agent to control devices, apps and code

items.summary: Months before Anthropic's record-setting IPO, Palantir CEO Alex Karp criticized frontier AI companies like Anthropic and OpenAI for pushing businesses toward dependence on their models. In a CNBC interview, Karp said "We have people trying to drug addict us to a future they [frontier AI models] believe they control," arguing that enterprises should retain ownership of data, infrastructure, and models rather than transferring value to third-party providers as part of Palantir's 'AI sovereignty' campaign. He characterized Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's vision as one "where we own nothing... where our adversaries win." The remarks drew support from Chamath Palihapitiya, who said Karp "deserves a medal," and Satya Nadella, while Jamie Dimon emphasized that companies would ultimately prioritize return on investment. Anthropic responded through Amodei's statement reaffirming its commitment to safety and human control, calling the industry a "race to the top." The comments also touched open-weight models—backed by Palantir in an July letter with Nvidia and Microsoft—and Karp's claim that frontier models derived value from distilling internet and enterprise intellectual property. These remarks gained renewed attention after Anthropic's IPO valued the company at nearly $2 trillion, with shares closing at $97.17, up 17% from its $83 offering price; Amodei stated this "strengthens our resolve to do the right thing." The figures are reported as facts by the article rather than forecasts.
items.title: Palantir CEO Alex Karp accused frontier AI labs of 'drugging' enterprises into dependency, resurfacing after Anthropic's IPO

items.summary: Jon McCormack retired from Apple at the end of October after more than eight years heading its Camera and Photos apps and underlying image-capture technology. No direct vice-president successor was named; his responsibilities are being absorbed by former deputies reporting to Sebastien Marineau-Mes, who now leads AI-integration efforts across Apple's operating systems, while key leaders such as Alok Deshpande remain on the camera team. McCormack oversaw features including the redesigned selfie camera with the iPhone 17 lineup and a variable-aperture camera on the iPhone 18 Pro models, plus a customizable professional Camera app interface during his tenure. He was known internally as an opponent of generative AI for creating or substantially altering photographs, telling Wired that "A photograph is of something that actually happened"; however, people familiar with the matter said his retirement was not tied to any disagreement over Apple's AI strategy. His departure adds to a period of transition in software engineering under Craig Federighi and joins Jennifer Bailey among vice presidents who left this fall, as new CEO John Ternus pursues efficiency-focused management changes.
items.title: Jon McCormack, Apple's iPhone camera-software chief, retires after eight years

items.summary: A New York Times report says Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in its largest public offering on record, selling 980 million shares at $83 each under ticker ANT; shares opened at $111.50. The article reports that some employees began buying homes months before the listing using expected shareholdings as backing and could sell about 10 percent of holdings on the first trading day. Real estate agents expect many to move into larger family-friendly homes in San Francisco neighbourhoods such as Noe Valley, Cole Valley and Potrero Hill, often through limited liability companies for privacy; this is contrasted with Facebook's 2012 listing, when engineers were seen driving expensive sports cars. Wealth managers report clients now asking about houses, furniture and helping relatives rather than luxury spending, though the article cautions that luxury spending may not disappear entirely. Seven co-founders have pledged to give away 80 percent of their equity, and Anthropic matches staff commitments to charitable causes; Wild Animal Initiative has received donations of about $100,000 and $50,000 from employees and is in talks over contributions worth millions, while the company announced $50 million in grants for local causes by end of 2027 and plans a public benefit fund starting with 5 percent of its shares. The windfall lands in an expensive market: San Francisco's median house price rose 29 percent to $2.39 million over a year, luxury sales hit nine homes above $10 million and 40 above $5 million in one month, mayor Daniel Lurie declared a rent emergency after apartment prices rose 26 percent, and some rent-controlled tenants are being offered large payments to leave; Redfin estimated that Anthropic and OpenAI employees could collectively afford nearly a third of homes in the San Francisco metro area, though this figure combines both companies and is hypothetical. Tipping Point Community's chief executive Sam Cobbs said he expected greater contributions but had not seen signs of broader commitment, and noted Anthropic gave nonprofits free access to its AI tools for six months before charging.
items.title: Anthropic's record IPO and how employees plan to use their wealth

items.summary: Bloomberg ranked Anthropic as the world's seventh most valuable publicly traded company, with a closing fully diluted valuation of about $1.8 trillion on its Thursday Nasdaq debut; Apple ($5.1 trillion), Microsoft ($3.7 trillion), Nvidia ($3.5 trillion), Alphabet ($3.3 trillion) and Amazon ($2.8 trillion) ranked higher, followed by SpaceX at $1.9 trillion. Shares opened at $111.50 (about 34% above the $83 IPO price), then pared gains to close at $97.17, up 17% from the offer price; the opening price briefly implied a valuation of about $2 trillion using roughly 18 billion shares including options and RSUs. The listing marked a sharp rise from an estimated $183 billion valuation around 14 months earlier, after Anthropic had sought slightly more than $1 trillion during its November roadshow. Profit-taking followed the early surge as investors weighed prospects against concerns over high AI valuations, infrastructure spending and long-term profitability; analyst Bob O'Donnell of TECHnalysis Research said stability would depend on OpenAI's performance, Nvidia developments, data center policy and Anthropic's historical results. Led by CEO Dario Amodei (a former OpenAI employee), the company reported 47% quarter-over-quarter revenue growth in Q3 with a narrowing net loss, holds nearly $900 billion in computing commitments with partners including Amazon and Google, and has indicated it may use debt toward investment-grade status. The valuation is based on Bloomberg's closing-price ranking of fully diluted market values; the figures are reported claims from Reuters and Bloomberg rather than independently verified data.
items.title: Anthropic's Nasdaq IPO valuation after profit-taking

items.summary: Pakistani think-tank analyst Khurram Abbas alleged on X that India did not extend the customary welcome to Pakistan climate change and environmental coordination minister Musadik Masood Malik, who arrived in New Delhi on Thursday for the first SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum. ANI cited official sources contradicting this claim, reporting that a director from the Union ministry of culture and an under secretary from the MEA's Pakistan, Afghanistan and Iran (PAI) division were present at the airport to receive Malik as part of welcome protocol. The same sources stated all SCO member countries arriving in New Delhi received similar treatment. Malik is described as the first Pakistani minister to visit India since 2023 and the first such trip following the May 2025 military confrontation after the Pahalgam terror attack, which killed 26 people; his last high-profile counterpart was foreign minister Bilawal Bhutto Zardari in 2023. Abbas's post characterised him as a Pakistani climate change and environmental coordination minister arriving to attend an SCO meeting, welcomed by the Pakistani CdA. The forum runs November 20-22, with Pakistan representing Islamabad on dialogue among civilisations; MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal confirmed invitations extended to all 10 member states plus observers and partners.
items.title: ANI contradicts Pakistani analyst's claim that no Indian official welcomed Musadik Malik in Delhi

items.summary: The Supreme Court on Friday dismissed Karnataka's appeal against a state high court ruling that allows bike taxi operations across the state, leaving in place an order benefiting Ola, Uber, Rapido, motorcycle owners and the Bike Taxi Welfare Association. The high court permitted motorcycles to be registered as transport vehicles and used as contract carriages provided they meet the state's regulatory requirements.
